name: Battle of Kulikovo
info: On 8 September 1380 the Russian forces of Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeated the army of Mamai of the Golden Horde at Kulikovo Field near the Don, though Mongol overlordship over Russia went on.

facts.date: 8 September 1380 (a Julian date, not converted); the Russian law of 1995 marks the victory on 21 September
facts.place: Kulikovo Field, near the mouth of the Nepryadva where it meets the Don, now in Tula Oblast, Russia; the exact ground is disputed
facts.sides: Russian principalities under Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow, with Vladimir Andreyevich of Serpukhov and Dmitry Bobrok-Volynsky commanding the ambush regiment; the Horde of Mamai, who was not a Genghisid and ruled through puppet khans. No source gives the numbers reliably: modern estimates for the Russians run from 6,000 or 7,000 to 36,000 and more.
facts.outcome: The Russians held the field and pursued the Horde for more than 50 kilometres. Mamai fled and was killed soon after, Tokhtamysh took the whole Horde, and in 1382 he burned Moscow.

t: The course of the battle rests on late tellings, above all the Tale of the Rout of Mamai from the 16th century, and no source from the Tatar side survives. Estimates of the Russian army run from 6,000 or 7,000 to hundreds of thousands in the chronicles.
A regiment hidden in an oak grove struck the Horde's flank when the Russian left and the great banner had given way, and the Horde broke and was chased more than 50 kilometres.
The victory did not end Mongol rule. Tokhtamysh, who gained most from Mamai's fall, sacked Moscow in 1382, and the Horde's overlordship was formally ended only in 1480.
dyk: The prince is said to have exchanged horses and armour with his boyar Mikhail Brenok so that he could fight as an ordinary boyar. Brenok was found dead under the great banner, and Dmitry was found among the corpses.
ev: Dmitry stops paying tribute to Mamai and open conflict between Moscow and Mamai begins
Mamai's army under Murza Begich is defeated by the Moscow forces at the Vozha River
Dmitry gathers an army at Kolomna and moves south, crossing the Oka and then the Don
The Russian army and Mamai's Horde fight at Kulikovo Field, opened by the duel of Peresvet and his Horde opponent
A regiment placed in ambush strikes the Horde and the Horde is routed and pursued to the Krasivaya Mecha
Khan Tokhtamysh takes and burns Moscow and Dmitry accepts him as sovereign
Dmitry leaves the grand princely throne to his son in his own will, without asking the khan
The Great Stand on the Ugra River formally ends Russian vassalage to the Golden Horde

sections.background:
After the Mongol invasion of Rus' in the 13th century the Russian principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde. Moscow grew in power and often challenged its neighbours. Dmitry Donskoy became prince of Moscow in 1359 at the age of nine, and by 1365 had forced the princes of Nizhny Novgorod to give up claims to the Grand Duchy of Vladimir. Mikhail of Tver received a jarliq (a khan's patent) for Vladimir from Mamai in 1371 and again in 1375, but Moscow's troops kept him out, and in 1375 Dmitry forced Tver to submit. A truce with Lithuania in 1372 recognised Vladimir as the hereditary possession of the Moscow princes.

In the Horde, the killing of Berdi Beg in 1359 began the Great Troubles. Mamai, his son-in-law and beylerbey, took power in the western part. He was not a Genghisid, so he enthroned khans of that line and ruled through them, always contending with rivals. Open conflict between Dmitry and Mamai began in 1374, though the exact causes are unknown; the puppet khans were by then plainly illegitimate and Mamai demanded more money as he lost the war for the Horde's throne. A Tatar force defeated the army of Nizhny Novgorod on the Pyana in 1377, but Begich's army was defeated on the Vozha in 1378. Meanwhile Tokhtamysh, who had the support of Tamerlane, took power in the east of the Horde.

In 1380 Mamai's envoys demanded tribute as in the time of Khan Jani Beg, and Dmitry offered only the sum of his earlier agreement with Mamai. Mamai allied with Jogaila of Lithuania and counted on Oleg of Ryazan, though Oleg's part is sometimes challenged.
sections.forces:
The earliest chronicle tales give no details of the Russian army's make-up. Gorsky, a Russian historian, reconstructed it from two chronicles he judges reliable: detachments from most of north-eastern Russia, part of the Smolensk princes and of the upper Oka principalities, and the Lithuanian princes Andrei of Polotsk and Dmitri of Bryansk, but none from Nizhny Novgorod or Tver. The lists of princes in the Tale of the Rout of Mamai, he holds, cannot be trusted. Russian sources give 150,000 to 200,000 men, or 300,000 and more, and historians have reduced these steadily: 100,000 to 150,000 (Maslovsky, 1881), 50,000 to 60,000 (Razin, 1957), at most 36,000 (Kirpichnikov, 1966), 6,000 to 7,000 (Dvurechensky, 2014), and 20,000 (Kuzmin).

The Russian army was formed into a Patrol (sentry), a Forward, a Right Hand, a Left Hand, a Large and an Ambush regiment, divided into about 23 banners. One account places the Large Regiment and Dmitry's court in the centre under the okolnichy Timofey Velyaminov, the Right Hand under Andrei of Polotsk, and the Left Hand under Vasily of Yaroslavl and Fyodor of Molozha. The Ambush regiment under Vladimir Andreyevich and Dmitry Bobrok stood in an oak grove; later tellings differ on which flank. Ravines guarded the flanks.

Russian sources give the Horde only as innumerable, and no Tatar source survives. Mamai hired mercenaries, and a later source gives a Genoese infantry in his centre, which Zhukov doubts. Modern figures for the Horde run from 7,000 (Dvurechensky) to 30,000 (Kuzmin) and 100,000 or more. Jogaila and Oleg arrived too late to take part.
sections.course:
Dmitry gathered his army at Kolomna and left on 20 August. He crossed the Oka at Lopasnya and moved south, reaching the Don on 6 September. A council decided to cross before the allies of Mamai could join him, though this cut off the way back. On the morning of 8 September, in thick fog, the army crossed the Don; according to the Nikon Chronicle the bridges were then destroyed. It took position on the clean field by the mouth of the Nepryadva, and the Tatars appeared and formed against it.

The Tale of the Rout of Mamai, which gives the fullest course, has the champions Alexander Peresvet and Temir-Murza (also Chelubey) open the battle: each killed the other with a spear. The main forces met, by the Expanded Chronicle Tale, at the sixth hour of the day. Dmitry, in the Tale's account, stood in the ranks in a boyar's armour and left his banner with the boyar Brenok. The fighting was long and the field too narrow for the Horde to use its mobility and flanking. The Tatars slowly gained ground, threw down the great banner and killed Brenok. The Left Hand regiment was overturned and the Russian army seemed close to rout.

Then the ambush regiment attacked the Horde's flank. People and horses, tired from the long fight, could not withstand fresh troops, and the Horde's line collapsed. The Russians pursued the Tatars more than 50 kilometres to the Krasivaya Mecha River. Dmitry was found among the corpses, exhausted.
sections.aftermath:
The losses were heavy. A third of the commanders of the 23 banners fell, among them the princes of Beloozero and Alexander Peresvet. For six days the victorious army stayed on the field among the dead. Later tellings report more than 500 boyars dead and 253,000 of the retinue, with 50,000 left; these figures are doubtful. Razin put the Russian dead at about 25,000 to 30,000, Kirpichnikov at about 800 boyars and 5,000 to 8,000 men, Urlanis at about 10,000, and Bulychev at about a third of the Russian force.

When Jogaila heard of Mamai's defeat he turned his army back to Lithuania. People of the Ryazan land attacked groups returning from the field, plundered them and took prisoners, whose return was still an issue in the Moscow and Ryazan treaties of 1381 and 1402. Dmitry prepared to punish Ryazan, Oleg fled, and he was later restored but accepted Dmitry as his older brother and signed a peace.

Muhammad Bolak, Mamai's puppet khan, was killed in the battle. Mamai escaped to Caffa in Crimea, raised a new army, and with no legitimate khan found his nobles going over to Tokhtamysh. He fled again to Crimea and was killed there. Tokhtamysh thereby united the Horde after a split of twenty years. In 1382 he marched on Moscow, took and burned it and made Dmitry accept him as sovereign.
sections.sources:
No source from the Tatar side survives; if any was written it was probably lost when Timur burned the archives of Sarai. Russian accounts are late or literary. The Short and Expanded Chronicle Tales are in chronicles of the 15th century, the Zadonshchina survives in manuscripts from the 1470s, and the Tale of the Rout of Mamai, which dates to the 16th century and survives in over a hundred copies, gives the most complete course, though it is not known whether it rests on an earlier source or is a later reconstruction. It places Metropolitan Cyprian in Moscow and Algirdas alive in 1380 and has Dmitry meet Sergius of Radonezh, which is almost certainly wrong. It and the Chronicle Tale also disagree on whether Dmitry was wounded and left the field or fought to the end unhurt. The Zadonshchina adds dead princes and the 253,000 fallen, which is doubted, and the duel of the champions may be legend.

The German chroniclers Johann von Posilge and Detmar of Lübeck wrote briefly of a battle on a river they call Blue Water, probably from Lithuanian informants. Ostrowski holds that these accounts are earlier and more accurate and show that the battle took place on the Don but was less significant than claimed.

The site is disputed. Medieval sources say only a clean field beyond the Don near the mouth of the Nepryadva. Archaeologists under Dvurechensky placed it in 2005 between the Nepryadva and the Smolka, while Azbelev argues for the river's source. Finds are few, including four spearheads and a piece of mail.
sections.legacy:
Most Russian historians since the 19th century have seen the battle as a liberation from the Tatar yoke. Others hold that it did not itself change anything fundamental but showed that Moscow had gained a dominant position in north-eastern Rus'. Solovyov saw it as a victory that stopped another invasion from Asia, with the meaning for eastern Europe of the battles of the Catalaunian Plains and Poitiers for the west. Some Western historians doubt that its importance should be stressed and call Tokhtamysh the real winner, a view Gorsky shares. Vernadsky wrote that, with the Horde's quarrels continuing, the battle would have brought immediate independence, but unity was restored soon after, and Russia could not meet the next trial after the heavy losses of 1380.

Moscow's rise went on. In 1389 Dmitry, in his will, left the grand princely throne to his son without the khan's patent, and the Horde had to accept the new grand prince. Payment of tribute became irregular. Dmitry took the name Donskoy after the battle, though by another view he received it only under Ivan the Terrible.

The battle produced the Kulikovo cycle of Russian literature, in which later versions grew more religious. A column was set up on the field in 1852, the 500th anniversary was held there in 1880, and a state museum-reserve was founded in 1996. A law of 1995 fixes 21 September as a day of military glory; this does not match the accepted date of 8 September.

summary: At Kulikovo Field near the Don on 8 September 1380 the Russian forces of Dmitry of Moscow defeated the army of Mamai of the Golden Horde, with an ambush regiment turning the fight. Numbers and course rest on late tellings, and Mongol overlordship continued until 1480.
notes: Numbers: every figure is attributed; the sources give from 6,000 to hundreds of thousands. The Russian army's figures in English and Russian articles differ for Dvurechensky (6,000 to 7,000 in the English; 8,000 Russian, 7,000 Mamai in the Russian).

Positions: English places Brenok at the head of the Large Regiment; Russian has Velyaminov commanding it and Brenok under the banner. I gave the Russian detail as one account and the Brenok detail as the Tale's.
Hour: the English article converts the sixth hour to about 10.35 am; the Russian says after midday. I gave only 'sixth hour'.

Oleg of Ryazan: the English says he sided with Mamai, 'although this fact is sometimes challenged'; the Mamai article says Ryazan was excluded from the Russian alliance. I wrote that Oleg was counted on by Mamai.

Left out: the Mamai article's claim that Muhammad Bolak was replaced by Tulak in 1379, while the Kulikovo article and the Russian one name Muhammad Bolak as the khan killed in the battle. Left as the Kulikovo article has it.
Left out: Kuchkin's view that Sergius's blessing belongs to the Vozha battle (no space), the Don icon legend, the Zadonshchina quotations.
A sentence on Gorsky in the English article ('larger than it was in the Kulikovo battle' for the 1375 army) was not used.
The English article's note that Dmitry 'fainted from exhaustion' is shortened to 'wounded and exhausted'.
